summary: Defines managed objects for subnetworks using IEEE 802.5 Token Ring technology, as an experimental part of the MIB. It was replaced by RFC 1743 and RFC 1748.

eli5.summary: It is a checklist for monitoring networks where computers pass a token around a ring to take turns.

questions: what is the token ring mib
what objects does the 802.5 mib define
subtitle: A set of SNMP-readable objects for monitoring and controlling IEEE 802.5 Token Ring interfaces.

tldr.problem: Network managers had no standard way to read the state, error counters and timers of IEEE 802.5 Token Ring interfaces over the network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an experimental MIB module with three tables (interface, statistics and timer) plus identifiers for interface tests and hardware chip sets.
tldr.outcome: It was later obsoleted by RFC 1743 and RFC 1748, and updated by RFC 1239 along the way, so it is no longer the current definition.

today: RFC 1231 was obsoleted by RFC 1743 and RFC 1748, and was updated by RFC 1239. Its status is listed as Proposed Standard, but the replacements are the definitions to look at.

sections.title: What This MIB Is For
sections.content:
RFC 1231 defines an experimental portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing subnetworks that use the IEEE 802.5 Token Ring technology, as described in IEEE Standard 802.5-1989. A MIB is the virtual information store that network management protocols read and change.

It builds on the Internet-standard Network Management Framework: RFC 1155 and RFC 1212 for describing objects, RFC 1213 (MIB-II) for the core set of objects, and RFC 1157 for the SNMP protocol used to reach them. The Framework permits new objects to be defined for experimentation and evaluation, which is why this module lives in the experimental namespace.
sections.eli5: This is a list of questions a network doctor can ask a Token Ring computer, such as how it is feeling and how many mistakes it has made.

sections.title: Three Tables and Some Identifiers
sections.content:
The module defines three tables. The 802.5 Interface Table holds state and parameter information specific to 802.5 interfaces. The 802.5 Statistics Table holds interface statistics. The 802.5 Timer Table holds the values of the timers that 802.5 defines.

A managed system has one entry in the Interface Table and one entry in the Statistics Table for each of its 802.5 interfaces. Implementing the Timer Table is optional, while the statistics table is described as mandatory for systems with 802.5 interfaces.

The memo also defines object identifiers: some name 802.5 tests for use with the ifExtnsTestTable, and some name Token Ring chip sets for use with the ifExtnsChipSet object, both from the interface extensions document it cites.
sections.eli5: There are three forms to fill in for each Token Ring connection: one for its current situation, one counting its mistakes, and an optional one listing its stopwatch settings.

sections.title: Scope and Naming
sections.content:
All objects are registered in one subtree of the experimental namespace, defined as dot5 OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= { experimental 4 }. They apply to every interface that conforms to the IEEE 802.5 specification, meaning interfaces whose ifType in the Internet-standard MIB is iso88025-tokenRing(9). For these interfaces, ifSpecific in MIB-II has the value of dot5.

The memo also introduces one textual convention, MacAddress, an OCTET STRING of 6 octets. It changes neither syntax nor semantics of any object, and exists only for the convenience of readers. The addresses use the canonical bit order of IEEE 802.1a, even though 802.5 itself transmits MAC addresses most significant bit first.
sections.eli5: Every Token Ring connection gets its own labelled folder in one shared filing cabinet, and addresses are written in one agreed way so everyone reads them the same.

sections.title: The Interface Table
sections.content:
Each interface entry is indexed by dot5IfIndex, which has the same value as ifIndex for that interface. The main objects are:

  • dot5Commands (read-write): set to open(2) to enter the ring, reset(3) to reset, close(4) to leave the ring, or no-op(1) for no effect. Reading it always returns no-op(1).
  • dot5RingStatus: a sum of values, one per current condition, such as 32 for Ring Recovery, 8192 for Soft Error, 32768 for Signal Loss and 131072 for no status because an open has not completed. A value of 0 means no problems were detected.
  • dot5RingState: whether the interface is opened, closed, opening, closing, openFailure or ringFailure.
  • dot5RingOpenStatus: the success or reason for failure of the latest attempt to enter the ring, for example lobeFailed, beaconing or duplicateMAC.
  • dot5RingSpeed (read-write): oneMegabit, fourMegabit, sixteenMegabit or unknown.
  • dot5UpStream: the MAC address of the upstream neighbor station.
  • dot5ActMonParticipate and dot5Functional: whether the interface takes part in active monitor selection, and the bit mask of functional addresses it accepts frames for.
sections.eli5: The first form tells you whether the computer has joined the circle, who stands just before it, how fast the circle spins, and lets you tell it to join or leave.

sections.title: Statistics and Timers
sections.content:
The Statistics Table holds error counters, each defined as a 32-bit wrap-around counter. If the hardware keeps 16-bit counters, the agent must read them often enough to avoid losing significance so that it can maintain 32-bit counters in software. Counters include dot5StatsLineErrors, dot5StatsBurstErrors, dot5StatsLostFrameErrors, dot5StatsSoftErrors, dot5StatsHardErrors, dot5StatsSignalLoss, dot5StatsTransmitBeacons, dot5StatsLobeWires and dot5StatsRemoves.

The Timer Table lists 802.5 timers, such as dot5TimerReturnRepeat and dot5TimerHolding, in units of 100 microseconds. Timer objects are read-only by default, but implementors are encouraged to offer read-write access where useful, giving due consideration to the dangers of writable timers.
sections.eli5: The second form is a tally sheet of every time something went wrong. The third lists how long each kid may hold the ball before passing it on.

sections.title: Tests, Chip Sets and Security
sections.content:
Under dot5Tests, the memo defines the Insert Function test, testInsertFunc. Invoking it makes the station test its insert ring logic if its lobe cable is connected to a wiring concentrator. The RFC warns that this inserts the station into the network and could cause problems on an operational network.

Under dot5ChipSets, it names three chip sets: chipSetIBM16, chipSetTItms380 and chipSetTItms380c16. Its Security Considerations section states only that security issues are not discussed in this memo.
sections.eli5: One test makes a computer step into the circle, which can disturb a game in progress, so the RFC warns you to be careful.
